title: When Some Qualities Need More Ratings Than Others
summary: The same rating budget buys different precision. In CLEAR-Bench, clarity needed about six times as many ratings as actionability to reach the same reliability reference.
body_markdown:
## Overview


In CLEAR-Bench, we took 2,848 model responses to consumer health questions and evaluated them across several dimensions at once, and in this last post in The Limits of Preference we use that depth to answer a question every rubric evaluation runs into, which is how many ratings a response needs before its score can reliably tell it apart from another.


Alongside the head-to-head preferences behind earlier posts in the series, crowd annotators rated every response for actionability, empathy, and clarity on the same three-point scale, yet the number of ratings each quality needs turns out to be very different. Actionability needs about three ratings per response to reach a reliability of 0.80, a common reference point, and clarity needs about eighteen.


That means an evaluation that collects the same ten ratings for every quality measures actionability at 0.93 reliability and clarity at only 0.69, so its clarity comparisons are much weaker for the same amount of work.


It's easy to assume annotators just disagree more about what makes a response clear, but they disagree about clarity about as much as they do about empathy. The responses are much closer together on clarity, so the same amount of disagreement hides the differences between them. If we give clarity empathy's level of annotator disagreement, its reliability only moves from 0.18 to 0.19, and if we give it empathy's spread between responses instead, it rises to 0.40.


When agreement looks low, the usual move is to tighten the rubric. That assumes the annotators are the problem, but on clarity they differed about as much as they did on empathy. What set clarity apart was how close together the responses were, and when responses are that close, what helps is more ratings per response.


**Figure 1.** Projected reliability of a response's average rating as more annotators rate it. At the 0.80 reference, actionability needs about 3 ratings, empathy about 6, and clarity about 18.


[View full size ↗](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5f7a53ddbb40d1e517cf0fa7/6b05ba711df127c7cac90a2a_6b05b87e490ac449025ce215_tlop-05-1.png)


Earlier in the series we separated answer features from model identity, tested whether people reject flawed answers, compared rubric changes with preference changes, and checked whether different annotator groups produce different rankings.


Every one of those analyses relied on having enough human judgments behind each comparison, and this post asks how many judgments are enough, using the actionability, empathy, and clarity ratings from the same benchmark.


## Study design


This post uses the 2,848 CLEAR-Bench responses, the same ones behind Parts 01 and 04, which came from four models answering 712 consumer health questions. Annotators rated each response on actionability, empathy, and clarity one at a time on a three-point scale, which is different from the head-to-head choices in Parts 01, 02 and 04. These ratings came from CLEAR-Bench's rating collection, which ran separately from its 26,780 head-to-head preference judgments and drew on a larger annotator pool than the 132 in Part 04.


In total we collected 101,034 ratings, and each one answered a single question.


For clarity, annotators rated each response as clear, somewhat clear, or unclear, and the other two qualities also used three ordered options. Actionability had 177 annotators, empathy had 305, and clarity had 299, with some overlap between the groups. Everyone included in this analysis passed our quality checks.


We scored each rating contest after it ended, so nobody got feedback while rating. That was deliberate because, on subjective qualities, feedback can push people toward one reading of the rubric, and we wanted each annotator’s own judgments.


## Agreement and reliability


Two annotators rating the same response give it the same actionability rating 74.1 percent of the time, compared with 52.3 percent for empathy and 47.4 percent for clarity.


Brackets show 95 percent intervals. The chance baseline accounts for how often annotators used each option, so each quality has its own baseline.


[View full size ↗](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5f7a53ddbb40d1e517cf0fa7/6b05ba711df127c7cac90a26_6b05b87e35e7fa48c6578f68_tlop-05-5.png)


Agreement shows how often two annotators give the same rating, but the question for this post is how well the ratings separate responses from each other.


For that we measure reliability with the intraclass correlation, or ICC, which is the share of all the variation in ratings that comes from differences between responses.


An ICC of 1 means every annotator rates a given response the same way, and an ICC of 0 means knowing which response someone rated tells you nothing about their rating.


Single-rating reliability: actionability 0.58, empathy 0.42, clarity 0.18.


[View full size ↗](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5f7a53ddbb40d1e517cf0fa7/6b05ba711df127c7cac90a2d_6b05b87e490ac449025ce231_tlop-05-2.png)


One actionability rating is about three times as reliable as one clarity rating, and each gap in that ranking is distinguishable from zero in an uncertainty analysis that treats annotators, rather than individual ratings, as the unit.


For clarity, only about a fifth of the variation comes from differences between responses, so any single clarity rating, from any annotator, carries less information, and averaging does the work.


Averaging several ratings improves precision because differences among annotators partly cancel out, and how fast it improves depends on where each quality starts.


At five ratings per response, actionability reaches 0.87 while clarity is at 0.53, and even at ten ratings clarity is still below where actionability is at five. Using 0.80 as a reference point, that works out to about three ratings for actionability, six for empathy, and eighteen for clarity, as shown in Figure 1.


The 0.80 reference is a common convention. It doesn't mean 80 percent of ratings are correct, that annotators agree 80 percent of the time, or that a response meets a clinical standard. It describes how well the average separates responses under this design. A higher or lower target would change the counts, but clarity would still need roughly six times as many ratings as actionability.


## How we calculate reliability


We treat the three rating options for each quality as points on a single scale, so every rating is a number and we can measure how spread out the ratings are. That spread has two sources, how much responses differ from each other and how much annotators differ when rating the same response, and we estimate each one as a standard deviation.


Single-rating reliability, the ICC, is the share of the total variance that comes from differences between responses. Variance is the standard deviation squared, so for clarity the calculation is 0.30² ÷ (0.30² + 0.64²), which comes to about 0.18. The same calculation gives about 0.58 for actionability and about 0.42 for empathy.


Averaging several ratings shrinks the annotator part of the variance while the differences between responses stay the same, so the average gets more reliable as ratings are added.


## Why clarity needs more ratings


**Figure 2.** Spread between responses and among ratings of the same response, as standard deviations on the three-point scale. Responses sit closer together on clarity, while annotators vary about as much on clarity as on empathy.


[View full size ↗](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5f7a53ddbb40d1e517cf0fa7/6b05ba711df127c7cac90a34_6b05b87e5acda178d29cd80a_tlop-05-6.png)


Responses differ about as much on actionability as they do on empathy (0.53 vs. 0.52), but annotators differ less when rating actionability (0.45 vs. 0.61), which makes actionability easier to measure.


On clarity, annotators vary about as much as they do on empathy (0.64 vs. 0.61), but the responses differ much less (0.30 vs. 0.52), so annotators are trying to detect smaller differences with about the same amount of disagreement.


Think about people rating office chairs for comfort. If one chair is much more comfortable than another, a few opinions will tell them apart even though people have different preferences.


If the chairs feel about the same, those same personal differences can hide the small gap between them, so you need more ratings even though the people rating them are just as good at judging comfort as before.


We check this by recalculating reliability with one estimated component swapped at a time.


Giving clarity empathy's spread between responses raises its reliability from 0.18 to 0.40, close to empathy's 0.42, while giving it empathy's annotator variation only moves it to 0.19. For actionability, giving it empathy's annotator variation lowers its reliability from 0.58 to 0.43.


**Figure 3.** What-if recalculations. Swapping in empathy's spread between responses lifts clarity's single-rating reliability from 0.18 to 0.40, while swapping in empathy's annotator variation moves it to 0.19.


[View full size ↗](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5f7a53ddbb40d1e517cf0fa7/6b05ba711df127c7cac90a31_6b05b87e261a901bc6aaf369_tlop-05-3.png)


These recalculations use the measured components directly, which pins down where the gap comes from. Whether the responses are more alike on clarity or annotators hold opposing preferences that partly cancel out, the answer for anyone running an evaluation is the same, clarity needs more ratings.


The CLEAR-Bench collection already adapted rating counts to each response, which kept collecting ratings until annotators reached an agreement-based stopping rule, and clarity's rule asked for the most. This analysis shows why that matters.


We started this series by asking people which AI answers they would rather receive, and following those judgments through five analyses showed how many separate decisions go into an evaluation. Every health AI evaluation should come with a defined quality, a relevant population, a comparison designed for the question you're asking, and enough judgments behind each score for the comparison to hold.
